content: The safety data for tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) during pregnancy is limited but suggests an excellent safety profile. However, TAF has not yet been approved for preventing mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of hepatitis B virus (HBV). Regarding maternal safety, a meta-analysis of six studies estimated an 8% risk of HBV flare after discontinuing tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), which is statistically comparable to the 6% flare rate observed in untreated women. Data on restarting antiviral therapy after postpartum flares remain limited. For infant safety, a randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluated the effect of TDF prophylaxis on infant bone mineral density compared to a placebo. No statistically significant differences were observed in lumbar spine bone mineral density at one year of age. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated for women taking TDF, as the drug is present in very low concentrations in breast milk and has shown no evidence of toxicity in infants exposed through breastfeeding. The FDA classifies TDF as a Pregnancy Category B drug, indicating no adequate evidence of risk in humans, while entecavir (ETV) is classified as Category C. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 131 studies across all WHO regions found that globally, 21% of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)-positive pregnant women had HBV DNA levels ≥200,000 IU/mL, with regional variations ranging from 8% in the Eastern Mediterranean to 31% in the Western Pacific. The global estimate of HBeAg-positive pregnant women was 24%, with regional variations from 9% in the Eastern Mediterranean to 34% in the Western Pacific. Among HBsAg-positive pregnant women, 23% had HBV DNA levels ≥200,000 IU/mL and were HBeAg-positive, while 76% had HBV DNA <200,000 IU/mL and were HBeAg-negative. The certainty of evidence was rated as moderate. Since 2020, the WHO has recommended TDF prophylaxis for HBsAg-positive pregnant women at high risk of transmitting HBV to their infants, particularly those with high HBV DNA levels (≥200,000 IU/mL) or positive HBeAg status. This prophylaxis should begin preferably at the 28th week of pregnancy and continue until at least delivery, in addition to providing timely hepatitis B birth-dose vaccination for all infants. However, significant challenges remain in accessing HBV DNA viral load or HBeAg serology testing, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, to determine eligibility for antiviral prophylaxis. No studies have yet examined the clinical impact and feasibility of expanding antiviral prophylaxis access to all HBsAg-positive pregnant women. To address this, the WHO commissioned a modeling study to evaluate different eligibility scenarios for antiviral prophylaxis. Modeling suggests that scaling up hepatitis B vaccination worldwide to 90% coverage, including a timely birth dose, could prevent an additional 14 million neonatal hepatitis B cases and 38,500 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) over the next decade. A recent modeling study across 110 countries assessed the impact and cost-effectiveness of universal TDF prophylaxis for all HBsAg-positive pregnant women in settings without access to HBV DNA testing. This strategy could prevent 5 million new neonatal HBV infections and avert 296,900 DALYs between 2024 and 2030, with the highest impact in the WHO African Region. The cost-effectiveness of hepatitis B prophylaxis guided by HBV DNA levels or HBeAg status varies by region. Prophylaxis for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL or positive HBeAg status is likely cost-effective in only 26% of 106 countries analyzed, including China, South Africa, and Vietnam. However, lower diagnostic and monitoring costs would make the strategy cost-effective in 70% of countries, including 24 in the African Region. Universal prophylaxis for all HBsAg-positive women, compared to a hepatitis B birth-dose strategy alone, would likely be cost-effective in 40% of countries. The 2020 WHO recommendation for TDF prophylaxis for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with high HBV DNA levels or positive HBeAg status is based on moderate-certainty evidence. This intervention is now a universal standard where HBV DNA testing is accessible. Most clinical trials supporting this recommendation evaluated maternal TDF prophylaxis alongside infant hepatitis B vaccination and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) administration. Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of immunoglobulin-free strategies based on maternal TDF prophylaxis and timely infant birth-dose vaccination. A systematic review found that all cases of MTCT occurred among women with high HBV DNA levels, even when infants received timely birth-dose vaccination, HBIG, and completed the hepatitis B vaccine series. In settings without access to HBV DNA or HBeAg testing, universal TDF prophylaxis could reduce MTCT risk alongside infant vaccination. However, no studies have directly compared the effectiveness of universal TDF prophylaxis versus targeted or no prophylaxis among HBsAg-positive pregnant women. In lowand middle-income countries with high HBsAg prevalence among pregnant women, universal TDF prophylaxis could address ongoing MTCT in the absence of HBV DNA testing. However, this approach requires careful monitoring of postpartum flares and potential risks associated with repeated interruptions of antiviral therapy. Expanding prophylaxis would also increase demand for antiviral therapy, necessitating robust procurement and supply chains. Universal prophylaxis may help compensate for suboptimal uptake of infant hepatitis B vaccination, particularly timely birth-dose administration, in highly endemic regions. However, most HBsAg-positive pregnant women do not have high HBV DNA levels and are not at significant risk of transmitting HBV to their offspring. Universal prophylaxis should only be considered in settings without access to HBV DNA testing, as targeted prophylaxis is more appropriate when testing is available. Scaling up hepatitis B birth-dose vaccination remains the most cost-effective intervention for preventing MTCT. Universal prophylaxis is intended to augment, not replace, timely birth-dose vaccination.
